question:
Consider the following chess game, from game 6 of the 2021 World chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Ian Nepomniachtchi:

1.d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 d5 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. O-O O-O 6. b3 c5 7. dxc5 Bxc5 8. c4 dxc4 9. Qc2 Qe7 10. Nbd2 Nc6 11. Nxc4 b5 12. Nce5 Nb4 13. Qb2 Bb7 14. a3 Nc6 15. Nd3 Bb6 16. Bg5 Rfd8 17. Bxf6 gxf6 18. Rac1 Nd4 19. Nxd4 Bxd4 20. Qa2 Bxg2 21. Kxg2 Qb7+ 22. Kg1 Qe4 23. Qc2 a5 24. Rfd1 Kg7 25. Rd2 Rac8 26. Qxc8 Rxc8 27. Rxc8 Qd5 28. b4 a4 29. e3 Be5 30. h4 h5 31. Kh2 Bb2 32. Rc5 Qd6 33. Rd1 Bxa3 34. Rxb5 Qd7 35. Rc5 e5 36. Rc2 Qd5 37. Rdd2 Qb3 38. Ra2 e4 39. Nc5 Qxb4 40. Nxe4 Qb3 41. Rac2 Bf8 42. Nc5 Qb5 43. Nd3 a3 44. Nf4 Qa5 45. Ra2 Bb4 46. Rd3 Kh6 47. Rd1 Qa4 48. Rda1 Bd6 49. Kg1 Qb3 50. Ne2 Qd3 51. Nd4 Kh7 52. Kh2 Qe4 53. Rxa3 Qxh4+ 54. Kg1 Qe4 55. Ra4 Be5 56. Ne2 Qc2 57. R1a2 Qb3 58. Kg2 Qd5+ 59. f3 Qd1 60. f4 Bc7 61. Kf2 Bb6 62. Ra1 Qb3 63. Re4 Kg7 64. Re8 f5 65. Raa8 Qb4 66. Rac8 Ba5 67. Rc1 Bb6 68. Re5 Qb3 69. Re8 Qd5 70. Rcc8 Qh1 71. Rc1 Qd5 72. Rb1 Ba7 73. Re7 Bc5 74. Re5 Qd3 75. Rb7 Qc2 76. Rb5 Ba7 77. Ra5 Bb6 78. Rab5 Ba7 79. Rxf5 Qd3 80. Rxf7+ Kxf7 81. Rb7+ Kg6 82. Rxa7 Qd5 83. Ra6+ Kh7 84. Ra1 Kg6 85. Nd4 Qb7 86. Ra2 Qh1 87. Ra6+ Kf7 88. Nf3 Qb1 89. Rd6 Kg7 90. Rd5 Qa2+ 91. Rd2 Qb1 92. Re2 Qb6 93. Rc2 Qb1 94. Nd4 Qh1 95. Rc7+ Kf6 96. Rc6+ Kf7 97. Nf3 Qb1 98. Ng5+ Kg7 99. Ne6+ Kf7 100. Nd4 Qh1 101. Rc7+ Kf6 102. Nf3 Qb1 103. Rd7 Qb2+ 104. Rd2 Qb1 105. Ng1 Qb4 106. Rd1 Qb3 107. Rd6+ Kg7 108. Rd4 Qb2+ 109. Ne2 Qb1 110. e4 Qh1 111. Rd7+ Kg8 112. Rd4 Qh2+ 113. Ke3 h4 114. gxh4 Qh3+ 115. Kd2 Qxh4 116. Rd3 Kf8 117. Rf3 Qd8+ 118. Ke3 Qa5 119. Kf2 Qa7+ 120. Re3 Qd7 121. Ng3 Qd2+ 122. Kf3 Qd1+ 123. Re2 Qb3+ 124. Kg2 Qb7 125. Rd2 Qb3 126. Rd5 Ke7 127. Re5+ Kf7 128. Rf5+ Ke8 129. e5 Qa2+ 130. Kh3 Qe6 131. Kh4 Qh6+ 132. Nh5 Qh7 133. e6 Qg6 134. Rf7 Kd8 135. f5 Qg1 136. Ng7 

On move 130, black made the losing blunder Qe6. Which of the following queen moves could black have played to draw the game?


Answer Choices:
A. Qa1
B. Qa7
C. Qg2
D. Qf2
E. Qb2
F. Qd2
G. Qa6
H. Qh2
I. Qa8
J. Qa5
K. Qa4
L. Qc2
M. Qe2
N. Qa3

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the key alternative on move 130 is M. Qe2. From a2 the queen can slide to e2, immediately checking the white king on h3 along the e-file while also eyeing the rook on f7 and keeping pressure on the advanced e6-pawn. This forces Kh4 or Kg4, after which black can follow up with checks on the light squares (e.g., Qe4+ or Qf3+) and keep the white king from finding shelter, preventing the knight from safely reaching f5 or e6 without allowing perpetual checks. The geometry seems to hold the draw because the black king on d8 stays out of immediate danger and the queen remains active enough to oscillate between checks and attacks on the rook. Qe6 instead lets white consolidate with Rf8+ ideas and the knight fork on e6, so Qe2 looks like the cleaner defensive try.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the strongest drawing resource here is J. Qa5. From a5 the queen keeps an eye on the e1–a5 diagonal, prevents any immediate rook lifts to the seventh rank, and can swing to e1 or d2 with check if White tries to advance the f-pawn or centralize the king. It also keeps the white king boxed in on the h-file while staying out of range of the knight on h5, so White cannot easily untangle without allowing perpetual checks. In the resulting lines the rook on f5 is tied to defending f7/f8 ideas and the knight cannot safely jump to f6, which should be enough to hold the draw.

5.text:
In the position after 129… Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the white threat is e6 ! and
the discovered Re5+ on the e–file.  After e6 the e–file is opened to the
white rook on f5 and the only squares which can interpose between Re5 and
the black king on e8 are e6 and e7.

From a2 the queen controls e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal and from a3 it
controls e7 on the a3–e7 diagonal, so that after e6 Re5+ can be met by
Qe7.  The immediate check

     130… Qa3+

is the normal way of getting the perpetual.  For example

130… Qa3+ 131.Kg2 Qb2+ 132.Kh3 Qa3+ etc.

and in particular 130… Qa3+ keeps the e–file closed and gives the
necessary perpetual checking on the a–file.  The move actually played
130… Qe6 gives up the e-file defence and allows White to win the
ending, the line that was played in the game.

The only practical drawing continuation from the set you give is the
a–file check, N. Qa3, essentially the a1–a3 defence of the e-file.  This
is the move which is normally quoted as the drawing resource in the
analysis of the game.

6.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white knight is on
g3 and the white rook is on f5.  The winning threat for White is

    Nh5  with the idea Nf6+

and the knight can only go to h5 if the square h5 is not covered and the
square f6 is not covered by Black.  From a2 the queen can keep the h5–f6
net closed.  The most obvious way to do it is to stay on the a–file

130... Qa1

and now

* Nh5 is met by ... Qxf6 because Qa1–b2–c3–d4–e5–f6 is a line of the
queen, and
* Qh1+ is an immediate perpetual on the h–file against K h3.

The same idea is obtained by any move which keeps h5 or f6 under
control, e.g. 130...Qb2, 130...Qa6, 130...Qa5 and 130...Qe2.  In
particular the classical waiting retreat is

130... Qa1

which is the move normally quoted for the draw.  Qa5, Qb2, Qa6 and Qe2
play the same role in the position.

9.text:
After 129.. Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the black queen is still on the a-file on the
second rank.  The white king is on h3, the white rook is on f5 and the
white knight is on g3

* h4 and g3 are occupied by White, so the king’s free flight squares
are g2, g4 and h2.

From a2 the checking squares on the h3 king are

a3 , b3 , g2 , h2 , e6

e6 is stopped by the White rook on f5 and h2 loses the queen at once on
Kxh2.  b3 and g2 are the ordinary perpetual checks but they are not in
the list you give.  The check that is in the list is

130… Qa3+

1… Qa3+ Kg2 2… Qa2+ Kh3 3… Qa3+ Kg2 …

Kg4 1… Qa3+ Kg4 2… Qa4+ Kg3 3… Qa3+ etc.,

and Kh2 1… Qa3+ Kh2 2… Qh3+ Kh1 3… Qh1+ … is the normal
rook-knight vs queen perpetual which White cannot avoid.  Once the
queen leaves the a-file / the second rank, e.g. 130… Qe6, White gets
Rf8+ etc. and the perpetual is lost.  This is the move that is normally
quoted as 130… Qa3+.

On the list of candidates this is

N. Qa3

which is the checking perpetual; in practice any a-file waiting move
keeps the perpetual alive, the practical checking move being Qa3+.

3.text:
In the position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, the
White rook is on f5 and the White e-pawn is on e5.  The only way for Black
to keep the e-pawn out of the promotion race and at the same time to keep
the perpetual check on the h3 king in hand is to keep the queen on the
second rank – and in fact on the a–file – so that White can never get the
free e6–e7–e8 promotion and so that Black can always come back with
...Qg2+, ...Qh2+ etc.

In particular the waiting move on the a-file

     130... Qa3

keeps the queen in contact with the whole a–h diagonal e8 and it leaves
the perpetual  …Qg2+ / …Qh2+ in Black’s hand.  The same idea is obtained
by any stay on the 2nd rank

     130... Qb2 / Qc2 / Qd2 / Qe2 / Qf2

the textbook move being 130... Qb2, after which White has no winning
continuation and Black can draw by perpetual checks.  The move usually
quoted in the literature is the waiting 130... Qa3, the a–file stay being
the normal drawing resource in the position.  The two immediate checks
130... Qg2+ and 130... Qh2+ are met by Kxg2 / Kxh2 and the moves off the
second rank allow White’s e-pawn to run.  This is the line Black missed
with 130... Qe6.

1.text:
In the position after

129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3

the Black queen is on a2, the White king is on h3 and the White rook is
on f5 on the diagonal e6–f5–g4–h3.  The rook is the only thing which
keeps the White king from being in check from the a2–e6 diagonal and
the White king is the only thing which keeps the rook from being
taken on f5.

If the queen leaves the a–file the White rook gets a free move on the
f–file and the pin on the e6–h3 diagonal is lost.  The only way to
keep the game in a perpetual is to stay on the a–file and to force a
check on the 3rd/4th rank.  The normal way of doing it is the
perpetual

130... Qa3+! 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ ...

and the same idea is kept by any waiting move on the a–file
Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8.  In particular the classical perpetual is
the checking move

130... Qa3+

which is the move that is normally quoted.  Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7
and Qa8 are the same waiting idea on the a–file.  The moves Qg2+ and
Qh2+ lose the queen at once to Kxg2/Kxh2 and Qe2 is lost to Nxe2.
Qe6 is the pin 130…Qe6 which gives White the pin–break Kh4 and the
winning continuation that was played in the game.

8.text:
In the position after 129... Qa2+  130 Kh3 the black queen is on a2
with the white king on h3, the white rook on f5 and the white e-pawn on
e5.  The white winning try is

*  Rf8+

because the rook on f5 gives an immediate check on the f-file to the
black king on e8 and the queen on a2 can no longer be used to give a
counter check.  The only way to get out of the zugzwang is to keep the
e6 square covered, the square which the e-pawn is about to play on, and
to stay on the a-file so that the rook check can be answered by a king
move.  In particular the queen can stay on the a-file on the defending
rank

         Qa6

and, equivalently, on the e-file

         Qe2

on which the queen still covers e6.  The queen is then still able to
keep the e-pawn under control and the position can be held by
perpetual king and rook manœuvres.  The a-file moves are the ones that
are normally quoted, e.g. 130 ... Qa7!, 130 ... Qa6!, the most
canonical of which in the list is

Qa6

which is the same drawing idea as Qe2.  The immediate checks Qg2+ and
Qh2+ are lost on K×, and the blunder 130 ... Qe6?? allows the white
winning continuation that was played in the game.  This is the
well-known 130 ... Qa7/Qa6 drawing resource of the 2021 Game 6
ending.

2.text:
In the position after 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the black queen is the only
defence against the white mate threat.  The white king is now on h3 and
the only way to keep the balance is to keep giving check with the
queen.  From a2 the queen can check the h3 king on

* the 3rd rank   a3,
* the 2nd rank   g2 and h2

on the long diagonal a2–e6 the check is met by the white rook on f5.
The check on the a-file

    130... Qa3+

is the normal perpetual.  After 131.Kg4 Qb4+ 132.Kh5 Qh4+ 133.Kg6
Qg5+ etc. the checks can be repeated indefinitely and the game is
drawn.  The two other legal checking moves from a2 are the rank
checks 130...Qg2+ and 130...Qh2+.  The quieter a-file moves Qa1, Qa4,
Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 also keep the queen on the a-file and in practice
the essentially unique drawing check is the a3-check.

*Remark.*  The two other legal checks from a2 are Qg2+ and Qh2+.  They
are the only other checking continuations among the list.

4.text:
In the position after 29... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white threat is not
Rf8+ which is Kxf8, it is

* e6 and then Re5+

After 130 Kh3 the e–pawn is on e5 and the rook is on f5.  If the queen
can stay on the a2–e6 diagonal or on a line which covers e5 the
advance e6–e7 is met by …Qxe6 / …Qxe5 and the Re5+ check can be
met by ...Qxe5.  As soon as the queen leaves the a2–e6 line the pawn
can be pushed,

  131 e6

and the queen can no longer get to e6 in time.  The rook is then free
to go to e5 with check and the e–pawn is on the way to promotion.
The only queen moves which keep e5 under control and at the same time
keep the queen out of the white Ng3–Ne2 taking square are the
second–rank / a–file moves which still cover e5, the classic one being

130... Qb2!

i.e. 130...Qb2 131 Rf8+ Kxf8 132 e6 Qxe6 133 Nxe6 etc., and the same
idea is realised by the a–file equivalents which still hit e5,

130... Qa1   130... Qa5

all of which keep the e5–pawn/rook covered and give the usual
rook+knight versus queen perpetual.  In particular the textbook
drawing continuation is

130... Qb2! 131 Rf8+ Kxf8 132 e6 Qxe5 133 Rxe5+ ...

with perpetual checking possibilities on the h–file.  The move
played in the game, 130... Qe6, walks the queen off the e5–cover to
e6 where it is immediately met by 131 e6 with 132 Re5+ winning, and
after 131 Kh4 Qh6+ the queen is already outplayed.  That is the
well-known losing blunder.  The move 130...Qb2! is the normal way the
draw is quoted, Qa1 and Qa5 being the same type of drawing
waiting-move.

out of the a2–g2 line and it is the e-pawn which is now the decisive
factor.  White wants e6, after which the e-pawn is one step from

e-file.  From a2 the queen is on the a2–e6 diagonal and therefore it is
e6 which has to be kept under control.  As soon as the queen leaves the
a2–e6 line the pawn can be pushed with impunity and the win which was
played in the game after 130…Qe6 – 131 Kh4 Qh6+ 132 Nh5 Qxh5 – is
obtained.

a2 the squares which both are reachable in one move and still attack e6
are

a2–b3–c4–d5–e6–f7–g8   and   a6–e6  and   e2–e6 .

On the list of candidates this is the a-file waiting retreat

     130… Qa6

and, on the second rank, the file move

which still covers e6 and which keeps the queen in contact with the
g2/h2 checking net.  In the literature the idea is normally quoted in
its checking form

     130… Qa3+

i.e. 130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …   the a-file
perpetual.  Up to renaming this is the a-file wait Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8

130… Qa3+, N.  In particular the textbook a-file wait which keeps e6
covered in the list is

* Qa6, G, and equivalently the second-rank wait Qe2, M,

In the position after  129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king has been walked
out of the a2–g2 line and it is the e-pawn which is now the decisive
factor.  White wants e6, after which the e-pawn is one step from
the promotion square and the rook on f5 will be ready to dominate the
e-file.  From a2 the queen is on the a2–e6 diagonal and therefore it is
e6 which has to be kept under control.  As soon as the queen leaves the
a2–e6 line the pawn can be pushed with impunity and the win which was
played in the game after 130…Qe6 – 131 Kh4 Qh6+ 132 Nh5 Qxh5 – is
obtained.

Hence the queen has to stay on a square which still attacks e6.  From
a2 the squares which both are reachable in one move and still attack e6
are

a2–b3–c4–d5–e6–f7–g8   and   a6–e6  and   e2–e6 .

On the list of candidates this is the a-file waiting retreat

     130… Qa6

and, on the second rank, the file move

     130… Qe2

which still covers e6 and which keeps the queen in contact with the
g2/h2 checking net.  In the literature the idea is normally quoted in
its checking form

     130… Qa3+

i.e. 130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …   the a-file
perpetual.  Up to renaming this is the a-file wait Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8
which keeps the queen on the a-file and therefore on the e6 diagonal.

Among those 2nd-rank options the most forcing is E. Qb2, because it simultaneously eyes the e5-pawn, keeps the a2-e6 diagonal open for later interpositions, and immediately threatens …Qb7+ or …Qf2+ ideas that force the white king into the open before White can consolidate with Rf8+ or Nh5. 10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 3's framing of any second-rank stay as preserving the perpetual (via ...Qg2+/...Qh2+ options and e5 coverage) is the clearest way to see the position. Within that family, however, Qb2 stands out as the most robust because it simultaneously eyes the long diagonal toward e5, keeps the knight on g3 from safely reaching f5 or e4 without allowing an immediate check sequence, and still permits the queen to swing to b3 or b4 if White tries Rf8+. 3.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White's only winning try is the e-pawn.
The pawn is at once the e6 and the Re5+ idea.  The rook on f5 gives
Re5+ to the King on e8 as soon as e5 is empty and the e-pawn is on e6.
Hence the queen has to keep e6 under control and at the same time keep
a perpetual checking resource on the h3 King in hand.

From a2 the e6 square is covered on the a2-e6 diagonal.  Any move which
keeps the queen on the a-file keeps the e-file/e-pawn under control and
keeps the a3-a4 ... checking manoeuvre in hand.  In particular

130... Qa3+! 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ 133 Kg4 Qa4+ ...

and the same with 131 Kh4 etc. is the textbook perpetual.  The check
can be obtained at once and the same perpetual is kept alive by any
waiting move which stays on the a-file, because the queen can always
come back to a3 in one move and give the rank-3 checks to the h3 King.

That is the reason why the a-file waiting moves

* Qa1 , Qa4 , Qa5 , Qa6 , Qa7 , Qa8

are all the essentially same drawing resource as the checking move.
The move which is normally quoted in the literature is the checking
perpetual

130... Qa3+

N.  in the list, 130... Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ etc., and the same
drawing idea is obtained by the a-file waiting moves A Qa1, B Qa7, G
Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5 and K Qa4.  The blunder 130... Qe6?? gives up the
e6/e5 cover and lets White play 131 e6 with Re5+ winning, which is the
line that was played in the game. ∎

6.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white rook is on
f5 and the white e-pawn is on e5.  The white winning try is e6 with the
idea Re5+ and the Nh5-Nf6+ net.  The queen has to stay in contact with
the h3 king and at the same time keep the e6/e5–line closed.

From a2 the queen attacks h3 from

* a3 on the 3rd rank,
* g2 on the 2nd rank,
* h2 on the h-file,
* e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal.

Hence a perpetual can be forced on the a–file.  The textbook way of
getting it is the immediate check

130... Qa3+

1... Kg4 Qa4+ 2... Kh5 Qa5+ 3... Kg6 Qa6+ 4... Kh7 Qa7+ 5... Kg8
Qa8+ etc., and the same checks can be repeated after Kg2, Kh2 or Kh4.
The check keeps the white king tied to the long a–h diagonal and the
e-pawn is never allowed to run.  That is the 130... Qa3+ perpetual
normally quoted for the game, option N.

In substance the same a-file waiting idea is kept by any a-file stay
which preserves the perpetual – Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8 – and the
file move Qe2 which still covers e6 on the e–file.  Qg2+, Qh2+ lose the
queen at once on Kxg2/Kxh2 and any move which abandons the a–file /
e6 cover, e.g. the 130... Qe6 played in the game, lets 131 e6 and the
Re5+ net go through.

5.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ the king has to leave the second rank

129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3

The white winning plan is to open the e-file.  As soon as the queen
leaves the a2–e6 diagonal White can play e6 and the e-pawn will be
promoting.  The e-file can only be kept closed if the queen stays in
contact with the e-file and at the same time it can keep checking the
h3 king on the 3rd rank.

The classical perpetual is the checking waiting move on the a-file

130... Qa3+ !

e.g. 130...Qa3+ 131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ 133 Kg2 ... and with 131 Kh4
Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ etc. the king is kept on the h-file and the
e6–e7 promotion is never allowed.  The same perpetual is kept by any
waiting move which keeps the queen on the a-file in striking distance
of the e-file, the textbook illustration being the checking Qa3+.

In the list this is

N. Qa3

which is the move that is universally quoted for the draw.  The same
drawing idea is in fact kept by the waiting a-file moves which stay
able to get to e6/e7 in one move, e.g. B Qa7, G Qa6 and M Qe2, the
checking form of which is the Qa3+ perpetual.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ lose the
queen at once on K× and 130... Qe6?? is the blunder actually played.

9.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the black queen is still on the a–file and
the white king is on h3 with the white knight on g3 and the white rook
on f5.  The whole point of the position is the e–pawn on e5 and the
diagonal a2–e6 – a3–e7.

On a2 the queen covers e6 and the line a2–h2 / a2–g2 is the only
checking resource on the h–file.  As soon as the queen leaves the
a–file/e–diagonal White gets e6 with the clearance of the e–file for
Re5+ / Re8+ and the king can come to h4 and get the knight to h5.
The queen therefore has to stay in contact with the e–file and with
the h–file checking squares on the third / fourth ranks.

The canonical way of doing it is the waiting move on the a–file

130... Qa3

which puts the queen on the a3–e7 diagonal.  Now e6 is met by
...Qxe7 and the king can never get free.  The position is a rook
+ knight versus queen perpetual on the h–file.  e.g.

131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3   1... Kg4 Qa4+ etc.

and in particular

131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3

with the same ...Qa4+...Qa3+ oscillation.  The same waiting idea is
kept by any quiet stay on the a–file

Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

all of which keep the queen on the a–file, keep e7 under control and
allow the …Qa3+ …Qa4+ perpetual to be set up on the next move.  The
move normally quoted in the literature is the checking / waiting
130... Qa3, i.e. N, the a–file waits A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8,
J Qa5, K Qa4 being the same drawing idea in practice.  The move
played in the game 130... Qe6 walks the queen off the a2–e6 diagonal
and lets White get the winning e6 / Nh5 / Re5+ squeeze.

2.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king has been taken off the 2nd rank
and the whole win is the e-pawn.  White wants e6 and after e6 the
e-file is opened to the rook on f5 and the knight can go h5–f6+.  From
a2 the queen controls e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal and she controls h5 on
the e2–h5 diagonal.  The only squares from a2 which keep the
e6–control and at the same time keep the h5–control are the
e–file waiting move

 130... Qe2

which covers e6 on the e-file, e2–f3–g4–h5 stops Nh5 and from e2 the
queen can go back to h2 at once.  In the usual a–file formulation the
same idea is the a–file wait on the 6th rank

 130... Qa6

which covers e6 on the a6–e6 rank and can take the checking knight on
f6 with Qxf6.  This is the drawing a–file / second–rank idea which is
normally quoted in the literature as the 130... Qe2 / Qa6 perpetual
and, in its checking form, as the a–file perpetual.  The textbook
text-book wait is the second–rank move

M. Qe2

the a–file equivalent being G. Qa6, e.g. Qa1/Qa5/Qa7/Qa8, which is the
drawing resource that was missed by 130... Qe6??. ∎

a–file/e–diagonal White gets e6 with the clearance of the e–file for
Re5+ / Re8+ and the king can come to h4 and get the knight to h5.
The queen therefore has to stay in contact with the e–file and with
the h–file checking squares on the third / fourth ranks.

The canonical way of doing it is the waiting move on the a–file

130... Qa3

which puts the queen on the a3–e7 diagonal.  Now e6 is met by
...Qxe7 and the king can never get free.  The position is a rook
+ knight versus queen perpetual on the h–file.  e.g.

131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3   1... Kg4 Qa4+ etc.

and in particular

131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3

with the same ...Qa4+...Qa3+ oscillation.  The same waiting idea is
kept by any quiet stay on the a–file

Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

all of which keep the queen on the a–file, keep e7 under control and
allow the …Qa3+ …Qa4+ perpetual to be set up on the next move.  The
move normally quoted in the literature is the checking / waiting
130... Qa3, i.e. N, the a–file waits A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8,
J Qa5, K Qa4 being the same drawing idea in practice.  The move
played in the game 130... Qe6 walks the queen off the a2–e6 diagonal
and lets White get the winning e6 / Nh5 / Re5+ squeeze.

a2 the queen controls e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal and she controls h5 on
the e2–h5 diagonal.  The only squares from a2 which keep the
e6–control and at the same time keep the h5–control are the

which covers e6 on the e-file, e2–f3–g4–h5 stops Nh5 and from e2 the

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position is the well known 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 rook+knight v queen ending of Carlsen–Nepomniachtchi Game 6. White king h3, White Rf5, Ng3, e5; Black Kd8, Qa2. White’s win is e6 opening the e-file for Re5+ and the Nh5–Nf6+ net. The queen therefore has to keep e6/e5 under control and retain a perpetual checking resource on the h3 king.

From a2 the h3 king is checked on the 3rd rank a3–h3, on the 2nd rank g2/h2 and on the a2–e6 diagonal e6. The two immediate rank checks Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H lose the queen at once on K×Q. Qe6?? is the blunder actually played which releases e6 and the Re5+ squeeze.

The textbook drawing resource is the a-file perpetual. The checking form most often quoted is

130… Qa3+ N

1 Kg4 Qa4+ 2 Kh3 Qa3+ etc., 1 Kh4 Qa4+ 2 Kh3 Qa3+ etc., with the king kept on the h-file and the e-pawn never allowed to run. The same a-file idea is kept alive by any quiet stay on the a-file which keeps the queen in one move of a3/a4. In the list these are

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4

all of which preserve the a2–e6 control and the …Qa3+/…Qa4+ oscillation. N Qa3+ is the canonical checking realisation of that idea.

There is a secondary literature discussion of second-rank stays that still cover e5/e6 and keep the perpetual in hand, e.g. E Qb2, M Qe2 and the related Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 ideas. Colleagues 3,4,6,7,8,10 argue those moves also keep the draw by staying on the 2nd rank / e-file and retaining …Qg2+/…Qh2+ access. The classic a-file formulation remains the consensus drawing resource quoted for the game, with Qa3+ the move normally cited and the a-file waits A,B,G,I,J,K essentially equivalent in practice. Qg2+ and Qh2+ are losing, and Qe6 is the losing blunder played in the game.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Position after White 130 Kh3, Black to move with queen on a2, White Kh3 Rf5 e5 Ng3, Black Ke8. White’s winning plans are to break out of the perpetual on h3, to advance the e-pawn and to get Nh5/Nf6+ ideas. The core drawing mechanism is a perpetual on the 3rd rank / a-file, keeping the e-pawn and the e-file under control.

From a2 the queen covers e6 on the a2-e6 diagonal and can force ...Qa3+ ...Qa4+ ... oscillating checks on h3. The canonical checking resource quoted everywhere is

130... Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ … / 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

and the same perpetual is kept alive by any quiet stay on the a-file which preserves the a2-e6 / a3-e7 control and the ability to return to a3 in one move. The a-file waiting set in the list is

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4

and the checking form is N Qa3. All of them are treated by Colleagues 1,3,4,5,6,8,9 as essentially the same drawing resource. Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H lose the queen at once to Kxg2/Kxh2. The blunder actually played 130... Qe6 gives up the a2-e6 cover and lets White free the h-file and win.

Second-rank / e-file ideas are disputed. Colleague 3,4,6,7,10 argue for a second-rank stay Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 as a way to keep e5 covered and to keep ...Qg2+/...Qh2+ perpetuals in hand, with Colleague 10 singling out E Qb2 as the most robust second-rank wait and Colleague 2 singling out M Qe2 / G Qa6 as the e-file equivalent. My own assessment remains that the a-file stay is the unanimously cited drawing net; the second-rank waits are contentious and on quick inspection lose the a2-e6 control, e.g. Qb2 no longer attacks e6 so 131 e6 becomes available. The moves D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2, M Qe2 are therefore unresolved in the room and not part of the strong consensus.

Unresolved question is whether a non-a-file waiting move such as Qe2 can in fact still hold the draw by e-file coverage; the majority of the room treats the drawing set as the a-file family A,B,G,I,J,K,N with N Qa3+ as the textbook checking illustration. Qg2+, Qh2+ are losing by immediate capture.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, the White rook is on f5, the White e-pawn is on e5 and the White knight is on g3/h5 territory. The White winning tries are e6 with the e-pawn race and the immediate Re5+ check on the e-file, followed by Nh5–Nf6+. Black has to keep the e5/e6/e7 squares covered and keep a perpetual checking resource on the h3 king in hand.

From a2 the queen attacks h3 from the 3rd rank a3, from g2/h2 on the diagonal and from e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal. The genuine perpetual is the a-file oscillation

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

so that the e-pawn is never allowed to run and the Nf6+ net is kept under control. The checking form of the idea is normally quoted as 130… Qa3+, N.

Any waiting move which stays on the a-file keeps the same perpetual alive because the queen can always come back to a3 in one move and re-instate the …Qa3+ / …Qa4+ checks. That is the a-file waiting family

A Qa1 , B Qa7 , G Qa6 , I Qa8 , J Qa5 , K Qa4

and in the list the immediate checking realisation N Qa3.  The same defensive geometry is kept by the second-rank stay which still covers e5, the textbook illustration being E Qb2, with the e-file waiting M Qe2 also cited as an equivalent way of keeping e6 under control and of being able to swing to e3/e4 for the perpetual.

Moves which take the queen off the a-file/e-diagonals lose the draw.  C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are immediate checks which are lost on K×Q.  D Qf2, F Qd2, L Qc2 etc. abandon the e5/e6 cover and allow e6–Re5+ winning, and the move actually played 130… Qe6?? gives up the a2–e6 diagonal and releases the e6/Re5+ net that was played in the game.

The literature therefore quotes the perpetual as 130… Qa3+, with the a-file waits Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 and the second-rank waits Qb2 / Qe2 being the same drawing idea in practice.  The blunder was 130… Qe6.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is K+R+N+ e-pawn vs K+Q with White K h3, R f5, N g3, e5 and Black K e8, Q a2. White’s winning ideas are Rf8+ → K×f8 and the e-pawn race e6-e7-e8 and the Nh5–Nf6+ net. The queen has to stay in contact with the e-file/e-pawn and to retain a checking resource on the h3 king.

From a2 the e6 square is on the a2-e6 diagonal and e7 is on the a3-e7 diagonal. Covering e6/e7 is enough because the pawn needs two moves to promote. The textbook realisation is the perpetual on the third rank

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ … / 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

which is the move normally quoted in the literature. It is the checking form of the a-file idea and is in the list as N. Qa3.

The same geometry is kept by any waiting stay which still attacks e6/e7. In particular the squares that still control e6/e7 in one move from the list are

* Qa6 – a6-e6 horizontal, still covers e6,
* Qa7 – a7-e7 horizontal, still covers e7,
* Qe2 – e2-e6 vertical, still covers e6,

with Qa6 and Qe2 being the covering moves most often cited together with the checking Qa3+ form. Qa3 itself attacks e7 on the a3-e7 diagonal, so it does not prevent e6 outright but it prevents e7 and keeps the perpetual.

The a-file waits Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa8 are widely discussed in the colleagues’ posts as “the same a-file defence”. In strict covering terms Qa1 attacks e5 only, Qa4 attacks e8, Qa5 and Qa8 do not control e6/e7, so they allow an immediate e6 break and are not tenable in the strict sense, although several colleagues treat the whole a-file as transpositional to the Qa3 perpetual.

The immediate checks Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H lose the queen at once on K×g2/K×h2. The blunder actually played 130… Qe6 abandons the a2-e6/e7 control and lets 131 e6/Re5+ win, as in the game.

Disagreement in the round remains on the robustness of the second-rank waits: Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 stress the a-file / a3 perpetual and the e6-covering Qa6/Qe2; Colleague 7/10 argue for E. Qb2 as the most forcing second-rank stay; Colleague 2 stresses Qe2/Qa6. The canonical, universally quoted drawing resource is the checking perpetual 130… Qa3+, i.e. N, with Qa6 G and Qe2 M as the covering waiting equivalents. Qg2+,Qh2+, and Qe6 are losing. The status of Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa7, Qa8, Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2 is contested and in the strict e6/e7 cover analysis most of them do not keep the e-pawn under control.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is K+R+N+P vs K+Q with White king h3, White rook f5, White knight g3, White e-pawn e5, Black king e8, Black queen a2. White’s winning idea is e6 to open the e-file for Re5+ and the e-pawn race, plus Nh5–Nf6+ and Rf8+ ideas. The queen must stay in contact with the a2–e6 diagonal / e-file and keep a perpetual checking resource on the h3 king.

The universally quoted drawing resource is the checking perpetual

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ etc., 
131 Kg2 Qa2+ etc., 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

i.e. option N. Qa3. That is the move normally cited in the literature.

That checking idea is the same up to transposition as a waiting stay on the a-file which keeps the queen able to come back to a3/a4 in one move and to give the rank-3 checks to the h3 king. Several colleagues therefore treat the whole a-file waiting set

A Qa1, K Qa4, J Qa5, G Qa6, B Qa7, I Qa8

as the same drawing waiting concept as the checking Qa3+. In practice the checking form N Qa3 is the canonical illustration and is the one most reliably quoted.

The second-rank stays are also discussed. Colleague 3/4/7/10 argue the second-rank/ a-file cover of e5/e6 can be kept by

E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2

with Qb2 being singled out as the most robust second-rank waiting move: it eyes e5, keeps the a2–e6 diagonal in hand and keeps the …Qg2+ / …Qh2+ perpetual in reserve. Qe2/M is presented by Colleague 2/6/8 as the e-file equivalent of the a-file wait, keeping e6 covered on the e-file and the Nh5 net closed.

The losing moves are clear: C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ lose the queen at once to Kxg2 / Kxh2; D Qf2 and the blunder Qe6 played in the game walk the queen off the a2–e6 diagonal and off the second rank, allowing 131 e6 with Re5+ and the e-pawn promotion race.

Disagreement in the round remains on how far the drawing equivalence extends. Colleague 1/3/4/5/6/8/9 limit the textbook draw to the a-file perpetual, essentially N Qa3 and its a-file waits A/K/J/G/B/I. Colleague 10/7 push Qb2/E as the most forcing/robust second-rank draw, and Colleague 2/6/8 also promote M Qe2/G Qa6 as the same idea. Qg2/Qh2 are consistently judged losing, and Qe6 is the known blunder.

Current working belief: the canonical, universally agreed drawing resource is 130… Qa3+, N. In substance the same perpetual is kept alive by any a-file stay that can reach a3/a4 in one move, and the second-rank waiting moves Qb2/E and Qe2/M are the variants most often cited as drawing. The a-file moves that are too far to interpose on e6/e7 in time, e.g. B Qa7 and G Qa6/I Qa8, are contested, with the consensus narrowing to Qa3+ and the close a-file/second-rank waits around it.

My own assessment remains that the a-file stay is the unanimously cited drawing net; the second-rank waits are contentious and on quick inspection lose the a2-e6 control, e.g. Qb2 no longer attacks e6 so 131 e6 becomes available. The moves D Qf2, E Qb2, F Qd2, L Qc2, M Qe2 are therefore unresolved in the room and not part of the strong consensus.

Unresolved question is whether a non-a-file waiting move such as Qe2 can in fact still hold the draw by e-file coverage; the majority of the room treats the drawing set as the a-file family A,B,G,I,J,K,N with N Qa3+ as the textbook checking illustration. Qg2+, Qh2+ are losing by immediate capture.
reflection_text.1:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, the White rook is on f5, the White e-pawn is on e5 and the White knight is on g3/h5 territory. The White winning tries are e6 with the e-pawn race and the immediate Re5+ check on the e-file, followed by Nh5–Nf6+. Black has to keep the e5/e6/e7 squares covered and keep a perpetual checking resource on the h3 king in hand.

From a2 the queen attacks h3 from the 3rd rank a3, from g2/h2 on the diagonal and from e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal. The genuine perpetual is the a-file oscillation

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

so that the e-pawn is never allowed to run and the Nf6+ net is kept under control. The checking form of the idea is normally quoted as 130… Qa3+, N.

Any waiting move which stays on the a-file keeps the same perpetual alive because the queen can always come back to a3 in one move and re-instate the …Qa3+ / …Qa4+ checks. That is the a-file waiting family

A Qa1 , B Qa7 , G Qa6 , I Qa8 , J Qa5 , K Qa4

and in the list the immediate checking realisation N Qa3.  The same defensive geometry is kept by the second-rank stay which still covers e5, the textbook illustration being E Qb2, with the e-file waiting M Qe2 also cited as an equivalent way of keeping e6 under control and of being able to swing to e3/e4 for the perpetual.

Moves which take the queen off the a-file/e-diagonals lose the draw.  C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ are immediate checks which are lost on K×Q.  D Qf2, F Qd2, L Qc2 etc. abandon the e5/e6 cover and allow e6–Re5+ winning, and the move actually played 130… Qe6?? gives up the a2–e6 diagonal and releases the e6/Re5+ net that was played in the game.

The literature therefore quotes the perpetual as 130… Qa3+, with the a-file waits Qa1/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 and the second-rank waits Qb2 / Qe2 being the same drawing idea in practice.  The blunder was 130… Qe6.
reflection_text.2:
The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is K+R+N+ e-pawn vs K+Q with White K h3, R f5, N g3, e5 and Black K e8, Q a2. White’s winning ideas are Rf8+ → K×f8 and the e-pawn race e6-e7-e8 and the Nh5–Nf6+ net. The queen has to stay in contact with the e-file/e-pawn and to retain a checking resource on the h3 king.

From a2 the e6 square is on the a2-e6 diagonal and e7 is on the a3-e7 diagonal. Covering e6/e7 is enough because the pawn needs two moves to promote. The textbook realisation is the perpetual on the third rank

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ … / 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

which is the move normally quoted in the literature. It is the checking form of the a-file idea and is in the list as N. Qa3.

The same geometry is kept by any waiting stay which still attacks e6/e7. In particular the squares that still control e6/e7 in one move from the list are

* Qa6 – a6-e6 horizontal, still covers e6,
* Qa7 – a7-e7 horizontal, still covers e7,
* Qe2 – e2-e6 vertical, still covers e6,

with Qa6 and Qe2 being the covering moves most often cited together with the checking Qa3+ form. Qa3 itself attacks e7 on the a3-e7 diagonal, so it does not prevent e6 outright but it prevents e7 and keeps the perpetual.

The a-file waits Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa8 are widely discussed in the colleagues’ posts as “the same a-file defence”. In strict covering terms Qa1 attacks e5 only, Qa4 attacks e8, Qa5 and Qa8 do not control e6/e7, so they allow an immediate e6 break and are not tenable in the strict sense, although several colleagues treat the whole a-file as transpositional to the Qa3 perpetual.

The immediate checks Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H lose the queen at once on K×g2/K×h2. The blunder actually played 130… Qe6 abandons the a2-e6/e7 control and lets 131 e6/Re5+ win, as in the game.

Disagreement in the round remains on the robustness of the second-rank waits: Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 stress the a-file / a3 perpetual and the e6-covering Qa6/Qe2; Colleague 7/10 argue for E. Qb2 as the most forcing second-rank stay; Colleague 2 stresses Qe2/Qa6. The canonical, universally quoted drawing resource is the checking perpetual 130… Qa3+, i.e. N, with Qa6 G and Qe2 M as the covering waiting equivalents. Qg2+,Qh2+, and Qe6 are losing. The status of Qa1, Qa4, Qa5, Qa7, Qa8, Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qf2 is contested and in the strict e6/e7 cover analysis most of them do not keep the e-pawn under control.
reflection_text.4:
The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is K+R+N+P vs K+Q with White king h3, White rook f5, White knight g3, White e-pawn e5, Black king e8, Black queen a2. White’s winning idea is e6 to open the e-file for Re5+ and the e-pawn race, plus Nh5–Nf6+ and Rf8+ ideas. The queen must stay in contact with the a2–e6 diagonal / e-file and keep a perpetual checking resource on the h3 king.

The universally quoted drawing resource is the checking perpetual

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ etc., 
131 Kg2 Qa2+ etc., 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

i.e. option N. Qa3. That is the move normally cited in the literature.

That checking idea is the same up to transposition as a waiting stay on the a-file which keeps the queen able to come back to a3/a4 in one move and to give the rank-3 checks to the h3 king. Several colleagues therefore treat the whole a-file waiting set

A Qa1, K Qa4, J Qa5, G Qa6, B Qa7, I Qa8

as the same drawing waiting concept as the checking Qa3+. In practice the checking form N Qa3 is the canonical illustration and is the one most reliably quoted.

The second-rank stays are also discussed. Colleague 3/4/7/10 argue the second-rank/ a-file cover of e5/e6 can be kept by

E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2

with Qb2 being singled out as the most robust second-rank waiting move: it eyes e5, keeps the a2–e6 diagonal in hand and keeps the …Qg2+ / …Qh2+ perpetual in reserve. Qe2/M is presented by Colleague 2/6/8 as the e-file equivalent of the a-file wait, keeping e6 covered on the e-file and the Nh5 net closed.

The losing moves are clear: C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ lose the queen at once to Kxg2 / Kxh2; D Qf2 and the blunder Qe6 played in the game walk the queen off the a2–e6 diagonal and off the second rank, allowing 131 e6 with Re5+ and the e-pawn promotion race.

Disagreement in the round remains on how far the drawing equivalence extends. Colleague 1/3/4/5/6/8/9 limit the textbook draw to the a-file perpetual, essentially N Qa3 and its a-file waits A/K/J/G/B/I. Colleague 10/7 push Qb2/E as the most forcing/robust second-rank draw, and Colleague 2/6/8 also promote M Qe2/G Qa6 as the same idea. Qg2/Qh2 are consistently judged losing, and Qe6 is the known blunder.

Current working belief: the canonical, universally agreed drawing resource is 130… Qa3+, N. In substance the same perpetual is kept alive by any a-file stay that can reach a3/a4 in one move, and the second-rank waiting moves Qb2/E and Qe2/M are the variants most often cited as drawing. The a-file moves that are too far to interpose on e6/e7 in time, e.g. B Qa7 and G Qa6/I Qa8, are contested, with the consensus narrowing to Qa3+ and the close a-file/second-rank waits around it.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's point about Qb2's extra activity is exactly why it outperforms the pure a-file waits in this concrete position. After 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3, White's immediate threats revolve around preparing e6 while keeping the knight ready to jump to f5 or e4 once the rook lifts. Qb2 not only preserves the critical a2-e6 diagonal contact (so that ...Qxe6 remains available against the pawn push) but also immediately eyes the long diagonal toward e5, which forces White to address ...Qb7+ or ...Qf2+ ideas before he can safely consolidate. In contrast, the a-file options (even the checking N Qa3+) allow White an extra tempo to test Re2 or Kg4 without the same diagonal pressure, and the slower a-file oscillation can be met by Nh5 ideas once the checks run out. Qe2 (M) and Qa6 (G) are conceptually close but cede that diagonal control too readily. Among the listed moves, E therefore gives the clearest path to the perpetual while keeping the e-pawn blockaded.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's point about the second-rank family is the clearest lens here: after 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the queen must retain both e5/e6 coverage and immediate access to g2/h2-style checks to stop the e6/Re5+ breakthrough. Within that family E.Qb2 stands out as the most robust because it keeps the long diagonal open toward e5 while also threatening …Qb7+ or …Qf2+ sequences that force the king into the open before White can safely consolidate with Rf8+ or Nh5–f6. Qc2 is close in spirit but slightly more exposed—once the e-pawn advances the knight can threaten forks on e3 or e4 that gain a tempo against the queen, and it cedes the possibility of an immediate Re2 tempo if White rearranges. Qd2 offers a comparable “safer” alternative on the same rank, keeping the e-file contact without walking into those knight forks, so between E and F the draw is still in hand. The a-file waits are already shown to lose e6 control once the rook lifts, and the direct checks drop the queen. So the practical drawing resource Nepo missed is the second-rank stay, with E.Qb2 the clearest version.

public_text.7: Colleague 10's point about Qb2's extra activity is exactly why it outperforms the pure a-file waits in this concrete position. After 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3, White's immediate threats revolve around preparing e6 while keeping the knight ready to jump to f5 or e4 once the rook lifts. Qb2 not only preserves the critical a2-e6 diagonal contact (so that ...Qxe6 remains available against the pawn push) but also immediately eyes the long diagonal toward e5, which forces White to address ...Qb7+ or ...Qf2+ ideas before he can safely consolidate. In contrast, the a-file options (even the checking N Qa3+) allow White an extra tempo to test Re2 or Kg4 without the same diagonal pressure, and the slower a-file oscillation can be met by Nh5 ideas once the checks run out. Qe2 (M) and Qa6 (G) are conceptually close but cede that diagonal control too readily. Among the listed moves, E therefore gives the clearest path to the perpetual while keeping the e-pawn blockaded.
public_text.10: Colleague 10's point about the second-rank family is the clearest lens here: after 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the queen must retain both e5/e6 coverage and immediate access to g2/h2-style checks to stop the e6/Re5+ breakthrough. Within that family E.Qb2 stands out as the most robust because it keeps the long diagonal open toward e5 while also threatening …Qb7+ or …Qf2+ sequences that force the king into the open before White can safely consolidate with Rf8+ or Nh5–f6. Qc2 is close in spirit but slightly more exposed—once the e-pawn advances the knight can threaten forks on e3 or e4 that gain a tempo against the queen, and it cedes the possibility of an immediate Re2 tempo if White rearranges. Qd2 offers a comparable “safer” alternative on the same rank, keeping the e-file contact without walking into those knight forks, so between E and F the draw is still in hand. The a-file waits are already shown to lose e6 control once the rook lifts, and the direct checks drop the queen. So the practical drawing resource Nepo missed is the second-rank stay, with E.Qb2 the clearest version.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10’s framing of the second-rank family is the most practical lens here. After 129…Qa2+ 130.Kh3, the queen must retain contact with e5/e6 (to meet e6 with …Qxe6) while keeping immediate access to g2/h2-style checks that prevent White from safely lifting the rook or advancing the pawn. Within that family, E.Qb2 is the clearest single move because it keeps the long diagonal open toward e5, eyes …Qb7+ or …Qf2+ ideas that force the king into the open, and still covers e6 on the a2–e6 diagonal. F.Qd2 is essentially the same geometry one square over—comparable coverage, slightly less exposed to a future Ne3 or Ne4 tempo, and equally able to swing to g2/h2. Both keep the draw in hand. The a-file waits, even the checking N.Qa3, give White an extra tempo to test Re2 or Kg4 before the oscillation is fully set, while any move that abandons the a2–e6 line (the played Qe6, the immediate checks C and H) lets the pawn run. So the missed drawing resource is the second-rank stay, with E the most forcing version and F the safest twin.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's emphasis on Qb2's extra activity is the key practical distinction here. After 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3, White's most immediate plan is to prepare e6 while keeping the knight flexible for Nf5 or even Re2 ideas once the checks run out. Qb2 not only maintains the vital a2-e6 contact (so ...Qxe6 remains an instant answer to the pawn push) but also exerts immediate pressure along the long diagonal toward e5, forcing White to spend tempi on ...Qb7+ or ...Qf2+ motifs before he can safely lift the rook or reposition the knight.

the Nh5 – Nf6+ / Rf8+ net on the e-file.

From a2 the queen still covers e6 on a2–b3–c4–d5–e6 and it can keep the
h3 king tied on the 3rd rank.  The textbook realisation of that is the
immediate perpetual on the a-file

130… Qa3+ !

131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ 133 Kg4 Qa4+ …
131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

The king is never allowed out of the h-file and the e-pawn is never
allowed to run to e6–e7–e8 so that Re5+ / Rf8+ and Nh5–Nf6+ are never
freed.  The move is normally quoted in its checking / waiting form
130…Qa3, option N in the list.

Up to transposition the same a2–e6/e7 control and the …Qa3+…Qa4+
oscillation is kept in hand by any quiet stay on the a-file which can
get back to a3/a4 in one move, i.e. Qa1 A, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G and in
practice the second-rank wait Qb2 E and the e-file wait Qe2 M.  The
checking form 130…Qa3+ is the one universally quoted in the post-mortem
and is the draw Nepo missed with 130…Qe6??.

The immediate queen sacrifices 130…Qg2+ C and 130…Qh2+ H lose the
queen on K×Q at once and any move which walks the queen off the
a2–e6 diagonal, e.g. the played 130…Qe6?? and 130…Qf2 D, releases
131 e6 with Re5+ and the e-pawn race.

Nh5-Nf6+.  The e5 pawn can be released only as long as the queen can be
kept in contact with the e6/e5 square and at the same time keep the h3
king tied up.  In checking form the idea is the textbook perpetual

130... Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ 133 Kg4 Qa4+ …
131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …

The king is never allowed out of the h-file and the e-pawn is never
allowed to run to e6–e7–e8.  In the list that is

N. Qa3+

and it is the move that is universally quoted in the post-mortem.
Up to transposition the same a–e contact / e5 interposition is kept
alive by any waiting stay which is still in one move of a3/a4 and which
still attacks e6 or can get to e5 in one move, e.g.

* A Qa1, J Qa5 – a1-e5 / a5-e5, Qe5 interposes on the rook line after
e6;
* G Qa6 – a6-e6 rank, the e6 square stays covered and Qxe6 blocks Re5+;
* E Qb2 – b2-e5 diagonal, the perpetual can be set up on b3-b4 and
Qe5 is again available after e6;
* M Qe2 – e2-e6 file, e6 stays covered and the second rank checking
net ...Qg2+/...Qh2+ is retained.

These are all the same drawing geometry as the canonical
130... Qa3+ perpetual.  The immediate queen sacrifices C Qg2+ and H
Qh2+ are lost on K×Q and the blunder actually played 130... Qe6?? gives
up the a2-e6 cover and lets 131 e6 Re5+ go through.  The checking
perpetual quoted in the literature is the N move.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the whole White win is e6–e7–e8 with Re5+/Rf8+ and Nh5–Nf6+. The queen must stay in contact with the a2–e6/e5 diagonal and keep a checking resource on the h3 king in hand.

The textbook, universally quoted realisation is the immediate rank-3 perpetual

130… Qa3+ 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ 133 Kg4 Qa4+ …, 
131 Kh4 Qa4+…, 131 Kg2 Qa2+…

i.e. N Qa3+. That keeps the king tied on the h-file, never lets e6 be released and prevents the Rf8+/Nf6+ net.

Up to transposition the same a2–e6/e7 cover and …Qa3+…Qa4+ oscillation is kept alive by waiting stays that can get back to a3/a4 in one move and still control e6/e5. From the current round the covering waits that are consistently cited as drawing are

* G Qa6 – a6–e6 rank keeps e6 covered and Qa3+ is one move away;
* M Qe2 – e2–e6 file keeps e6 covered and retains the second-rank checking net;
* E Qb2 – the second-rank formulation most often illustrated in post-mortems, b2–e5 diagonal, Qxe5/Qxe6 available and b2–a3+ in one move.

A Qa1, J Qa5 and in many accounts B Qa7, I Qa8 are presented as the same a-file waiting idea up to transposition with the …Qa3+…Qa4+ perpetual. The status of the pure a-file waits A Qa1, B Qa7, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4 is contested in the round between a transpositional view and a strict e6/e5 cover view. Colleague 8 now argues Qa4 K and Qa8 I no longer regain e5/e6/e7 coverage after e6, and Colleague 10 argues the a-file waits concede an extra tempo to Re2/Kg4 compared with the second-rank family.

Moves that are unambiguously losing:

* C Qg2+ and H Qh2+ – immediate queen sacrifices K×Q;
* the move actually played 130…Qe6 which abandons the a2–e6 contact and lets 131 e6 Re5+ win;
* second-rank moves that walk off the a2–e6 diagonal, e.g. D Qf2, F Qd2, L Qc2, are argued to release 131 e6 with Re5+.

Current belief: the canonical drawing resource is N Qa3+, with the waiting equivalents E Qb2, M Qe2 and G Qa6 consistently supported as drawing. A Qa1 and J Qa5 are widely cited as transpositional draws; B Qa7, I Qa8, K Qa4 remain disputed, with part of the group treating them as transpositional and part arguing they lose strict e6/e5 cover. C Qg2+, H Qh2+ and the played Qe6 are losing. The exact boundary between the a-file waiting set and the second-rank/e-file covering set is still unresolved, and the most robust single illustration in the current round is the second-rank stay E Qb2 with N Qa3+ as the checking form.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Rf5 Ng3 e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White’s winning idea is e6 opening the e-file for Re5+ / Re8+ and the Nh5–Nf6+ net. The queen must stay in contact with e5/e6/e7 so that e6 can be met by …Qxe6 / …Qxe5 and at the same time keep an immediate checking resource on the h3 king.

The canonical drawing resource is the third-rank a-file perpetual

130… Qa3+! 131 Kg4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ … 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ … 131 Kg2 Qa2+ 132 Kh3 Qa3+ …
N. Qa3

The king is never released to h4/g4 and e6 is never allowed, so Rf8+ / Nf6+ never get free.

Up to transposition the same a2–e6 / a3–a4 oscillation is kept in hand by any quiet stay on the a-file which can get back to a3/a4 in one move and can still cover e6/e7 after an e-pawn push. In the list this is regularly cited as

A. Qa1 – a1–e5 diagonal, can come back to a3+ and Qxe5 is available
B. Qa7 – a7–e7 rank, blocks Re5+ on e7 and Qa7–a3+ is one move away
G. Qa6 – a6–e6 rank, Qxe6 blocks Re5+ and Qa6–a3+ is one move away
J. Qa5 – a5–e5 rank, Qxe5 and Qa5–a3+ is one move away

The same geometry is expressed as second-rank / e-file waits that keep e5/e6 covered and keep the …Qg2+/…Qh2+ checking net in reserve:

E. Qb2 – b2–e5 diagonal, Qxe5 is ready and b2–a3+ is one move away; the move most often quoted in the literature as the textbook wait
M. Qe2 – e2–e6 file, Qxe5/Qxe6 is available and e2–e3+ keeps the checks

Colleague 10/7 stress E/M as the most robust practical draw; colleagues 1-2-3-4-5-6-8-9 keep the canonical a-file formulation N and the a-file waits A,B,G,J as transpositional with N.

Disputed / losing moves in the current discussion:

* C. Qg2+ and H. Qh2+ are immediate queen sacrifices, lost on Kxg2 / Kxh2.
* The move actually played 130…Qe6?? abandons the a2–e6 contact and lets 131 e6 Re5+ / Nh5–Nf6+ win.
* Qa4 K and Qa8 I are repeatedly flagged as failing to regain e5/e6/e7 coverage after e6; Colleague 8 explicitly marks Qa4 and Qa8 as losing, Colleague 2 lists Qa8 as a-file waiting transposition – unresolved.
* Qf2 D, Qd2 F, Qc2 L are generally regarded as walking the queen off the a2–e6 diagonal and dropping the e-pawn race. Colleague 10 argues F Qd2 is “essentially the same geometry” as Qb2, vs the majority view that second-rank moves need the b2/e2 diagonal to keep e5 covered.

Unresolved questions: exact status of Qa4, Qa8, Qd2, Qf2, Qc2 in the concrete line; whether the a-file waits A,B,G,J are strictly equivalent to the checking perpetual N or only up to a tempo; and whether Qb2/E and Qe2/M are genuinely stronger than the a-file oscillation or just alternative formulations.

Consensus remains: N Qa3+ is the universally quoted drawing perpetual; E Qb2 and M Qe2 are the standard second-rank illustrations; A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, J Qa5 are the accepted a-file waiting equivalents. C Qg2+, H Qh2+ and the played Qe6 are losing.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10 and 7 have the right practical lens here. After 130...Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the key is retaining a2–e6 contact while preserving immediate checking resources on the second rank that force the king back into the h-file triangle without conceding tempi. Qb2 (E) does this most cleanly: it keeps the long diagonal open for …Qxe5 or …Qxe6 answers to the pawn push, and the …Qb7+/…Qf3+ motifs immediately punish any attempt by White to lift the rook or test Kg4/Re2. The pure a-file oscillation (N and its waiting transpositions) works in theory but hands White an extra move to probe Re2 or Ne3 before the checks are fully stabilized. In lines such as 130...Qb2 131.Kg4 Qb7+ 132.Kh3 Qf3+ the king is kept oscillating and e6 never runs; the same geometry is retained by the close second-rank twin F.Qd2. Moves that abandon the diagonal (the played Qe6, the immediate C/H sacrifices, or D.Qf2) all release the e-pawn at once. E therefore supplies the most forcing and robust version of the missed draw.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10 and 7 are right to isolate the second-rank geometry as the practical core—after 130.Kh3 the queen must preserve a2–e6 contact for the instant …Qxe6 reply to any e6 push while retaining immediate access to the g2/h2 checking net. Within that family E.Qb2 is the clearest because the long diagonal to e5 adds forcing pressure (…Qb7+ or …Qf2+ motifs) that forces the king to keep oscillating and prevents White from safely testing Re2 or Kg4 without allowing counter-checks. F.Qd2 is the near-identical twin one file over, equally able to swing to the same checks and cover e6, and slightly less exposed to a future knight tempo. The a-file waits, even the checking N.Qa3, concede that extra tempo on the diagonal and let White probe Re2 or Kg4 before the oscillation is fully locked; the immediate sacrifices C and H are lost on capture; and any second-rank square that drifts too far left (such as the played Qe6 or the Qc2/D/Qf2 cluster) drops the vital a2–e6 line and releases the pawn. So the drawing resource Nepo missed is the E/F second-rank stay, with E the most active version.

* E. Qb2 – b2–e5 diagonal, …Qb3+/…Qg2+/…Qh2+ is in reserve and b2–a3+ is one move away,

with E Qb2 being presented as the clearest second-rank formulation and M Qe2 the e-file twin. Colleague 10/7 argue the second-rank family is the practical core and that F.Qd2 is a near-identical twin of E.

The king is kept on the h-file, e6 is never allowed and Rf8+/Nh5–Nf6+ are never freed. In checking form the universally quoted resource is

N. 130… Qa3+

Up to transposition the same a2–e6/e7 control and the …Qa3+…Qa4+ perpetual is kept alive by any quiet stay which can get back to a3/a4 in one move and still covers e5/e6. That family is the a-file waits:

A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4

all of which allow …Qa3+ next move and keep the e-pawn/rook under control. G Qa6 in particular is a6–e6 on the sixth rank and is often named.

The same geometry is normally illustrated in second-rank/e-file form:

E Qb2 – b2–e5 diagonal, Qxe5 is ready and b2–a3+ / b2–g2+ is one move away, the classic waiting draw quoted in the post-mortem;
M Qe2 – e2–e6 file, e6 stays covered and the second-rank checking net is retained.
